title: Client and server
short: One side asks, the other answers: the shape of every app.
what: A client is the program in the user's hands: a browser or a phone app. A server is a computer that waits for requests and sends back responses. They talk over the network, usually with HTTP: one request in, one response out.
analogy: Ordering at a coffee counter. You ask for a latte, the barista makes it and hands it over. The barista serves everyone in line and never walks up to you first.

frames.say: Your phone runs a weather app: the client. A server in a data center holds the forecasts. They talk only over the network.
You open the app. It sends a request, a short text message to the server's address: GET /forecast?city=Paris.
The server is always on, listening. It reads the request, checks that Paris is a real city, and works out what data it needs.
It asks its database for the Paris forecast. The database sits in the same building, so this takes about 2 ms.
It sends back a response: status 200 OK plus the data, temp 14 and rain 60%. Your phone draws the screen. Total trip: about 120 ms.
The same server answers thousands of phones and laptops. Each request carries everything needed, so the server treats them all alike.

when: Anything with users on phones or browsers
Data must be shared by many users
Logic or secrets can't live on the user's device
Someone asks what happens when you open a URL
python:
import json, threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.request import urlopen

class Weather(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):          # the server side
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"city": "Paris", "temp": 14}).encode())

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Weather)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
with urlopen(f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}/forecast?city=Paris") as r:   # the client side
    print(r.status, json.loads(r.read()))
watch: Never trust the client: check every input again on the server.
Each request is a round trip; on phones, a few big requests beat many small ones.
Keep login state in a database or cache, not in one server's memory, so any server can answer.
interview: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
